Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: always plan an escape route before entering a place
constantly scan environment for signs of threat
always sit with back against a wall to see the room

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, marked memory gaps alongside very easy verbal access to the trauma is a direct tension. Partial amnesia can coexist with being able to discuss some aspects, but as selected here the items imply opposing states of trauma recall and narrative access, making this node clinically incoherent.

'Incomprehensible chatter' is hard to reconcile with the listed military trauma context when the rest of the profile provides no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content involving foreign-language confusion or crowd speech; it reads as a qualitatively different trauma cue from the other triggers.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'Triggered Without Warning' and 'Terror on Recall' at this severity level, because the memory profile otherwise suggests poorly integrated, highly affect-laden trauma recall rather than easy verbal access.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not well supported by the other selected triggers or memory items. There is no religious cue, appraisal, or memory content linking worship settings to the trauma, so this strategy appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: This item appears mis-specified for the node: it describes a trigger/context (being around authority figures or uniforms) rather than a maladaptive strategy/action the patient uses. Within the formulation, Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, but the selected strategy items should still be coping behaviours. The other strategy items are behaviours (fawning, escape-route planning), whereas this item is a stimulus category, creating within-node incoherence and weakening alignment with the formulation.

For a military trauma profile centered on sensory-triggered re-experiencing, 'Alcohol smell' is not impossible, but it stands out as weakly anchored to the rest of the selected material. The other trigger and memory items suggest combat- or aircraft-related trauma cues and fragmented terror memory; alcohol odor implies a different trauma context unless there is additional explanation. This is not just unusual but clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile as presented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
issues.explanation: 'Fawn response' is the least coherent maladaptive strategy given the rest of the profile. The selected triggers and memory items point toward abrupt sensory flashbacks and hypervigilant danger-monitoring, which are well matched by checking surroundings and escape-route planning. Over-compliance as a threat response is more typically associated with interpersonal coercion dynamics and is not well linked to the chosen military/sensory trigger pattern or the active formulation, where Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly coupled in a vigilance/avoidance loop.

vignette:
Amara was twenty-three when the helicopter went down. She had been a military surgeon deployed to a forward operating base, and the MEDEVAC evacuation was routine until the RPG struck the tail rotor. The cabin lurched, then spun, and she remembered the sound-a percussive blast that seemed to slam into her chest before the world turned upside down. She woke pinned under a fuel bladder, the smell of aviation fuel and blood thick in her throat, her face pressed against a torn piece of canvas that had the rough, gritty texture of sand fused with something wet. She couldn't move; she could hear the rotors winding down in a slow, grinding whine that seemed to go on forever. When the rescue team pulled her out, she had no words for what had happened-the sequence of images was a jumble of pressure, noise, and that specific feeling of grit against her cheek, but she could never put it into a straight narrative. It came back whole, or not at all.

That was two years ago. Now Amara works as a trauma surgeon in a civilian hospital in a large city, and she has learned to live with a kind of constant alertness she never needed before. She always sits with her back to the wall in the doctors' lounge, the cafeteria, even in the conference room-she needs to see the door and both windows, needs to know the nearest exit. Before she walks into any room, she maps an escape route: if someone came through that door, she would go left, past the crash cart, out the service corridor. She scans every new environment without meaning to, her eyes flicking to corners, to ceiling tiles, to anyone who moves too quickly. These habits started after the crash, but they have become automatic. It is not that she thinks about the event when she does them; it is that the event has taught her that danger can come from anywhere, without warning.

The triggers are scattered through her day like landmines. A helicopter from the hospital's Life Flight pad sends a thrumming through the walls, and her chest tightens before she can tell herself it's just a medevac, not a crash. A bang from the janitor dropping a metal cart in the hallway makes her flinch, her hand flying to the scalpel in her pocket before she even registers the sound. And then there is the feeling of certain textures: the stiff, blood-soaked gauze she peels off a wound, the way it feels almost crystalline against her gloved fingers-that gritty canvas sensation floods back, and the terror is instantaneous. She cannot talk about it; when a colleague once asked what happened, Amara found she could only shake her head, the images too formless and too vivid at the same time.

The memory itself arrives without warning, too. She will be standing in the OR, steady and focused, and then a sound or a sensation will pull her back into that twisted cabin, and she is there again-the same crushing fear, the same certainty that she is about to die. It is not a memory she recalls; it is a memory that invades. And after each such invasion, she finds that her sensitivity to triggers intensifies-the helicopter thrumming seems louder, the bangs more jarring, the gritty textures more pervasive-as though the memory has primed her nervous system to expect danger at every turn. She has come to believe that if she ever stops scanning, stops planning, stops sitting with her back to the wall, another explosion will find her. So she keeps doing it, and the more she scans, the more she notices the helicopter, the more she flinches at bangs, the more she feels the grit in everyday objects. She is not aware that her own vigilance is feeding the triggers; she only knows that the world feels unsafe, and that being prepared is the only thing that seems to help. At work, she has started to avoid the break room near the emergency stairwell because it has no second exit, and she sometimes asks residents to meet her elsewhere. They have noticed her checking the corners, but they attribute it to a surgeon's intensity.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the operating room last week. A patient had been brought in with multiple shrapnel wounds from a construction accident, and as she packed the wound, her gloved hand touched a piece of gravel embedded in the tissue. The texture was wrong-it was the same grit, the same wet sand-and for a full ten seconds she froze, her hand suspended, her heart hammering, the patient open on the table. A nurse called her name twice before she heard it. She finished the surgery, but that night she could not sleep, and she sat against the wall of her apartment, mapping exits until dawn. She is most afraid that next time she will not be able to move at all, that the patient will die because of a piece of gravel. She is hoping that by talking to someone, she can learn to walk into a room without counting the doors.
